name: Convento do Carmo and Archaeological Museum
tagline: The roofless Gothic church left standing after the 1755 earthquake, now a small archaeology museum in Chiado

description.short: The ruined church of the Convento do Carmo, open to the sky since the 1755 earthquake, houses the Museu Arqueológico do Carmo. It is on Largo do Carmo in Chiado, about 1.7 km (25 minutes) from the ship with a steep final climb. Closed on Sundays; €7 adult.
description.full:
The Carmo ruins are one of the most striking sights in central Lisbon and one of the easiest to fit into a half-day ashore, as long as you plan the climb and remember the museum is closed on Sundays.

The Gothic nave lost its roof in the 1755 earthquake and was never rebuilt, so today you walk between the arches under open sky. The old chancel and side chapels hold the Museu Arqueológico do Carmo, a small museum run by the Association of Portuguese Archaeologists.

From the ship it is about 1.7 km. The first part is flat: walk west along the river to Praça do Comércio (14 minutes) and up Rua Augusta through the Baixa. The last part is a steep climb to Largo do Carmo. You have two ways up. Walk up Rua do Carmo and Calçada do Sacramento, about 10 minutes. Or take the metro Blue Line from Santa Apolónia to Baixa-Chiado, where escalators bring you up to Chiado, a few minutes' walk from Largo do Carmo. The Elevador de Santa Justa, whose top walkway leads almost to the door, has been closed since September 2025 with no reopening date.

Inside, allow 30 to 45 minutes. Walk the nave first, then the chancel rooms: Roman and medieval stone carving, the tomb of King Fernando I, azulejos and, the item most visitors remember, pre-Columbian mummies from Peru.

Crowds are moderate compared with the castle or Belém, and the busiest hours are around midday. The nave is open to the weather, so expect sun or rain inside.

For a short port call, combine it with Chiado and walk back down through the Baixa to the river. It is closed on Sundays, 1 January, 1 May and 25 December, which catches out many cruise passengers.
description.history: Nuno Álvares Pereira, the general who secured Portugal's independence from Castile, founded the Carmelite convent in 1389 and later lived here as a friar. On the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, the earthquake brought down the church roof. Rebuilding began in the late 18th century but stopped in the 1830s when religious orders were abolished, leaving the nave open. In 1864 the Association of Portuguese Archaeologists set up its museum in the ruins. On 25 April 1974 the prime minister, Marcelo Caetano, took refuge in the GNR barracks next door on Largo do Carmo and surrendered there, ending the dictatorship.
description.significance: Most of Lisbon was rebuilt after 1755; the Carmo nave is one of the few places where you can see the destruction itself. It is also a compact museum of Portuguese archaeology, and Largo do Carmo, outside the door, is where the 1974 Carnation Revolution came to its end. Three layers of Lisbon's history in one small square, 25 minutes from the ship.

directions.general: Located in Largo do Carmo square in Chiado, reached on foot uphill from Rossio and the Baixa, or a few minutes' walk from Baixa-Chiado metro
directions.fromCruisePort: About 1.7 km and 25 minutes on foot. Walk west to the Baixa, then up Rua do Carmo and Calçada do Sacramento (steep, about 10 minutes). The Elevador de Santa Justa has been closed since September 2025. Taxi about 8-10 minutes.
directions.publicTransport: Metro: Baixa-Chiado station (Blue/Green lines), Chiado exit, then a few minutes' walk to Largo do Carmo. Bus: 758. Tram: 28 passes nearby.
directions.parking: Extremely limited. Nearest parking at Restauradores or Portas do Sol. Not recommended to drive.

openingTimes.currentStatus: Open Monday to Saturday; closed Sundays

admissionPrices.notes: Adult €7. Full-time students with ID €5. Seniors 65+ with ID €5. Lisboa Card holders €5 (reduced, not free). Children 0–14 free with an adult. Groups over 30 people €5 each. Portuguese residents €5. Free for visitors with reduced mobility (60%+ disability certificate) plus one companion, and for ICOM card holders. Source: museuarqueologicodocarmo.pt.

visitingInformation.bestTimeToVisit: At 10:00 opening or after 16:00 on weekdays. Midday is busiest.
visitingInformation.adviceForVisitors: Closed on Sundays. Photography is allowed without flash or tripod. Half the visit is effectively outdoors, so dress for the weather. Large suitcases must be left at reception, subject to space. Combine with Chiado and walk back down through the Baixa to the river.

cruisePassengerInfo.timeNeededFromPort: About 2 hours: 25–30 minutes each way (the last stretch uphill) plus 30–45 minutes inside
cruisePassengerInfo.accessibility: The museum is wheelchair accessible inside, but the approach is a steep climb from the Baixa. Use a taxi, or the metro to Baixa-Chiado and its escalators, to avoid the hill.
combinableWith: Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara
Walk back down through the Baixa to Praça do Comércio
tips: Closed on Sundays, 1 January, 1 May and 25 December: check your port day before planning around it.
Open Monday to Saturday 10:00–19:00 from May to October (last entry 18:40) and 10:00–18:00 from November to April (last entry 17:40).
Adult ticket €7; students and over-65s with ID €5; children up to 14 free with an adult.
The Lisboa Card gives a reduced €5 ticket here, not free entry.
The Santa Justa lift is closed: walk up Rua do Carmo and Calçada do Sacramento (about 10 minutes, steep) or take the Blue Line to Baixa-Chiado and its escalators.
Payment is by cash (euros only), debit or credit card, or MB Way.
No flash or tripods, and large wheeled suitcases must be left at reception if there is space.
The nave is open to the weather: bring a hat in summer and an umbrella in winter.

highlights: Roofless Gothic nave, open to the sky since the 1755 earthquake
Museu Arqueológico do Carmo, founded in 1864
Roman and medieval stone carving, including the tomb of King Fernando I
Azulejo panels and Gothic architectural fragments
Largo do Carmo, where the 1974 Carnation Revolution ended
A few minutes' walk from Baixa-Chiado metro, which removes most of the climb
facilities: Brochures in Portuguese, English, Spanish, French, Italian, German and Japanese
Guided tours (ask at the ticket desk for the next one)
Limited space at reception for large bags

accessibility.mobilityNotes: The museum states that all public areas and entrances are wheelchair accessible, with an accessible toilet. The difficulty is getting there: Largo do Carmo is at the top of a steep hill. A taxi to Largo do Carmo is the simplest step-free option. Free entry for visitors with a disability certificate of 60% or more plus one companion.
